questions.q: What is the central symbol of the quill in "Mother Tongue," and what does it represent in the context of the Dogri language?
questions.a: The quill symbolises the Sharade script — the native writing system of Dogri that evolved from Brahmi — and represents the means to record, preserve, and transmit the language. A wrong answer (e.g., "the quill is just a pen") reveals the student is reading literally and missing the extended metaphor that links the physical object to cultural survival.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the speaker feels a sense of urgency when asking the reed for a quill.
questions.a: The urgency stems from the historical displacement of the Sharade script by Persian and later Devanagari scripts, leaving Dogri without a secure written form; the speaker fears the language will disappear if not written down immediately. A wrong answer that cites only "she needs to write quickly" shows the student has not connected the personal plea to the sociolinguistic context provided in the textbook's "About the Poet" note.

questions.q: Apply the concept of personification to analyse how the reed's dialogue ("Are you some sort of an accountant / With some Shah / Writing account books / Where you need a new pen / Every other day") characterises the relationship between the speaker and the script.
questions.a: The reed's personified voice initially treats the speaker as a bureaucratic functionary serving a worldly master (Shah), highlighting how the old script views its users as transactional; this contrast makes the revelation that she serves a "Shahni" (mother tongue) more powerful, reframing the request as devotional rather than clerical. A wrong answer that merely lists the personification without interpreting the Shah/Shahni contrast shows surface-level application.

questions.q: Analyse how the shift from "Shah" to "Shahni" in the speaker's reply restructures the power dynamic in the poem and what this reveals about the theme of linguistic ownership.
questions.a: The shift replaces a patriarchal, commercial master (Shah) with a nurturing, authoritative mistress (Shahni), transferring ownership of the script from external rulers to the intimate, maternal figure of the mother tongue itself; this reveals that true linguistic preservation comes from emotional ownership, not administrative imposition. A wrong answer that treats Shah/Shahni as mere vocabulary misses the gendered, cultural reorientation central to the theme.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the poem's ending — "The reed cut off its hand / Gave it to me and said / Take it / I too am her servant" — in conveying the message of collective responsibility for language preservation.
questions.a: The ending is highly effective: the reed's self-mutilation ("cut off its hand") dramatises sacrifice, and its declaration of shared servitude expands the duty from the individual poet to all elements of the culture (nature, history, community), making preservation a collective covenant. A wrong answer calling it "just a sad ending" fails to evaluate the structural move from individual plea to communal vow.

questions.q: Create a four-line stanza in free verse that uses a different central metaphor (not quill/reed) to express the same theme of urgent devotion to an endangered mother tongue.
questions.a: Example: "I knelt at the loom's empty frame, / Begging the shuttle for one last thread — / 'Weave me the words my grandmother spoke,' / The warp sighed, 'I am yours, unbroken.'" A poor answer that merely describes the theme without a sustained metaphor shows the student cannot transfer the poetic strategy to a new vehicle.
